subsystems.name: application
subsystems.capability: The application itself: routes, routers, app state, lifespan, and errors rendered as RFC 9457 problem details
subsystems.policy: Configuration is how Wreath starts; state is what it holds while running. They do not share an API. Route tables compile at startup, never per request. Dispatch is chosen at compile time too: `_select_dispatch` picks `_handle_http_plain` for an application with no global hooks and no dynamic matcher, and every delegation from it back to `_handle_http` must be decided *before* the specialized path has any effect a second dispatch would repeat -- before the Request exists, before a hook could run, before the recorder is told anything. A route handler may be `def` as well as `async def`; dispatch calls it and awaits only what came back awaitable, and every wrapper (binder, response validator, status coercion) preserves whichever convention it was handed. `_reject_session_after_authentication` scans **every** route-scoped registration -- `add_middleware`, `Router(middleware=[...])`, an included router's, and one route's `middleware=[...]` -- not just the application's. It used to read `self._middleware` alone, so a session middleware on a router walked past a refusal that had nothing to look at and shipped the 401 it exists to prevent (a check that has nothing to check). Nesting needs no special case: `Router.routes` folds an included router's middleware into each route before the application sees it. A global middleware may expose `applies_to(method, path)`, consulted once per route at compile time; routes it declines dispatch through a program compiled without it, so declining costs nothing per request. `_select_dispatch` then picks `_handle_http_compartment`, which routes *before* running the tape -- legal only because `classify` needs no Request, and only for an application with a classifying table, no dynamic matcher (host routing matches on a Host `ProxyHeaders` may rewrite) and no stage hooks. Per request it handles only `classify == 1`: a miss, an auth ticket, an armed recorder or an ambiguous path all hand back to `_handle_http` and run the full tape, so a rate limiter still counts 404s. Per-route programs are keyed by `(method, handler)` -- a multi-method route with no route middleware compiles to one shared endpoint object, and method is the axis compartments are most wanted on. `Wreath(middleware="native")` opts into `middleware.tape`, which records at boot every answer a configured `CorsPolicy` can give a preflight and lets `_wreath_http` serve them before the tape, before routing and before a `Request` exists. The table is recorded by *asking the middleware*, never by rebuilding its answer beside it -- reconstruction missed the `content-type` a 204 inherits from the Response class default, and the recorded answer must include the middleware's own egress hook, which is where a 403 refusal picks up `access-control-allow-origin` (so refusals are recorded per origin). Each probe runs twice and a middleware whose answers differ is declined. An origin outside the table falls through to Python rather than being refused, because `CorsPolicy`'s normalized compare accepts spellings the table does not carry. Opting in is a documented ordering change: middleware registered before CORS stops seeing preflights.

subsystems.name: routing
subsystems.capability: Startup-compiled static, parameter, trailing-path and host routing; named reverse lookup; declarative routers; and generic ASGI application mounts
subsystems.policy: One native PolicyRouteTable owns static, single-segment parameter, host-pattern and final {name:path} routing plus capability classification. Python materializes declarations before startup compilation and a handler only after native activation. Router inclusion remains declarative flattening; Wreath.mount is the explicit request-time ASGI composition surface.

subsystems.name: http
subsystems.capability: Requests and responses, application-owned trust-aware client IP and User-Agent/Client Hints facts with bounded Wreath-owned country and UA databases, request caching, verified Web Bot Auth identity fusion, automatic metrics and native Flight/OTLP projection plus pluggable rich fact providers, streaming and server-sent events, multipart file uploads, background tasks, and content negotiation over JSON, MessagePack and Protocol Buffers
subsystems.policy: Client facts ships data as well as readers: `country.wgd` is a 19,996-byte WGD2 image containing 2,281 exact IPv4 ranges across 251 countries and 318 exact IPv6 range runs; it never widens a range, so a miss is unknown rather than a guessed country. Sorted range gaps and inclusive spans are unsigned varints with a shared country table. Construction expands them once into operation-owned native arrays and builds 256-way first-byte directories, reducing lookup to a narrow binary search before Python receives only the final country code. `user_agent.wua` is a 4,969-byte WUA1 vocabulary with 197 entries spanning major and regional browsers, in-app clients, HTTP/cloud SDKs, monitors, feeds, search crawlers, AI training/search/user agents, and crawler frameworks; construction builds an operation-owned native hash table and lookup scans the header once. WGD2 refuses images over 20,000 bytes and WUA1 refuses images over 5,000 bytes. Richer country, city, coordinate and ASN facts remain pluggable through `GeoIPProvider` and `GeoIPRecord`; the framework surface names no data vendor. Request.stream is one-shot and enforces max_body_bytes as chunks arrive; body() buffers through that same stream and may be replayed, while consuming stream() first makes later body/json/form reads raise StreamConsumed. Multipart form parsing is incremental and spools a file at the threshold without retaining a whole-request body. PROTOBUF stays out of DEFAULT_SERIALIZERS -- JSON and MessagePack encode whatever a handler returns, protobuf can only encode a declared @message, and a handler returning a dict is the common case -- but a route whose *return annotation* is a @message has said at startup that its body is encodable, so `binding.compile_message_negotiation` makes the offer for that route and no other. It is compiled before compile_response_validator, because the validator projects onto JSON primitives and the encoder needs the message; a Response already passes that validator untouched, which is how the negotiated result reaches the wire without a second path. JSON stays what a missing Accept and */* resolve to, because adding an offer must not change what an existing client receives, and only an explicit protobuf win is intercepted -- an unsatisfiable Accept is left to the ordinary path rather than becoming a new 406. The generated OpenAPI advertises both media types on the request body and the response for such a route, spelled from negotiation.PROTOBUF so the document and the wire cannot name different types. `websocket.Calls` puts request/response on a frame pipe: `reply_to` and `label` are the protocol seam and neither has a default, because a guessed correlation field is a protocol the class does not know it is implementing. It is the single reader `WebSocket` documents, so a handler using it must not also iterate the socket; sends take a lock because a request and a reply genuinely race. A reply nobody awaits is ordinary, a second reply cannot settle a done future, a malformed frame does not end the loop (the calls outstanding on that socket are still answerable), and close fails outstanding calls rather than letting each wait out a deadline for an answer that provably cannot arrive. The bounded map is `_correlation.Pending`, shared with wreath.entity rather than written twice.

subsystems.name: edge
subsystems.capability: A reverse proxy and in-memory load balancer: peak-EWMA, round-robin or least-connections selection over a pool of upstreams, passive ejection with an exponential cooldown, retries for idempotent methods, and the hop-by-hop and forwarding-header hygiene a proxy owes the hop behind it
subsystems.policy: NATIVE-ONLY, BY DESIGN, and the first thing to know about this subsystem. Do not add a Python path. For a reverse proxy a Python fallback is a footgun, not a safety net: it degrades silently by ~5x (117 CPU-us per forwarded request against single-threaded haproxy's 25.7) in the one component whose whole job is to beat the thing in front of it, and nothing at runtime announces which path was taken. `serve()` is the native proxy and the shape everything else is measured against: a `loop.create_server` protocol that parses a request head in place, selects an upstream from the compiled table, writes the outbound head to an already-open upstream transport and relays the response back -- no scope, no Request, no coroutine, no Task. It takes no ASGI app, and that absence is the design: an app is the seam Python returns through. Upstream connections are opened while the proxy is being configured because `loop.create_connection` is a coroutine, and reaching for one mid-request drags asyncio's Task and Future machinery back onto the path. `ReverseProxy` remains for what `serve()` refuses -- TLS upstreams, retry onto a second upstream, upgrades -- and is the ASGI proxy, slower by construction. Do not migrate `ReverseProxy` leaf by leaf: moving the header transform alone into C was tried and measured nothing (113.2 against 110.1-117.2), because the primitives were never the cost. The Python that remains is configuration (Upstream, Ejection, UpstreamPool, DestinationPolicy): startup-only, compiled into the native structures once, free per request. Anything the native path cannot do yet is refused when the pool is constructed, naming what is missing -- never a slow path at request time. Correctness is checked differentially against haproxy and nginx rather than against another implementation of ours, because two of ours can be wrong in both halves and still agree. A build without the extension refuses at import with a named error. Mutation sweeps one mode. Upstream selection, health and in-flight counts are memory: no request-path database call decides where a request goes. PostgreSQL is where desired state would belong, and that half is not built. Every upstream is chosen once before any scoring runs -- a cold upstream's latency is a guess, and without that rule it starves permanently the moment a warm upstream measures faster than the guess. A pool with every upstream ejected still returns one, because refusing while every origin is briefly ejected is an outage of the proxy's own making and the declined request is the one that proves recovery. Only idempotent methods -- or a request carrying `Idempotency-Key` -- are retried on a second upstream, and only before the response head has been read, since after that a retry would deliver a prefix twice. `Host` and `Content-Length` are recomputed rather than relayed: the outbound framing must describe what this proxy actually sends, which is the egress half of the request-smuggling defence. `X-Forwarded-For` is replaced where `Via` is appended, because the first is an authorization input every parser reads leftmost and the second is a chain.

subsystems.name: http-client
subsystems.capability: Outbound HTTP with pooling, rate limiting, retries and Flight Recorder replay; service-to-service calls; bot challenges; and provider-native signed webhooks (Wreath, Standard Webhooks, Stripe and GitHub)
subsystems.policy: A buffered native HTTP/1 stream owns response-head parsing, content-length/chunked/close-delimited framing, trailer bounds, and header/body phase deadlines for the complete request operation. Python receives one final ClientResponse and retains the portable asyncio StreamReader transport path for conforming non-Wreath event loops; it never reparses bytes already held by the native stream. Pooling, destination policy, retries, redirects and service policy remain application-owned configuration around that transaction. BotChallenge.verify and WebhookVerifier.verify are the provider seams; challenge dependencies and WebhookSource layer over those public protocols, never concrete providers or private verifier methods.

subsystems.name: binding
subsystems.capability: Typed request and response contracts, rich stdlib scalars, reusable Field constraints and aliases, startup-compiled validation, and dependency injection with Depends
subsystems.policy: Native body validation executes a plan compiled once in Python; binding.validate remains the reference and native must match it byte-for-byte (errors included). Field numeric bounds, length bounds, patterns and aliases are native tape operations over the same traversal that constructs nested dataclasses. Recursive dataclasses and rich scalar annotations the tape cannot fully represent fall back to the Python validator; a partial native interpretation is forbidden. Supported return annotations filter, validate and serialize plain handler values; explicit Response objects retain wire ownership.

subsystems.name: openapi
subsystems.capability: A strict OpenAPI 3.1 contract derived from runtime validation, explicit responses and security, compatibility comparison, a self-contained docs UI, and generated typed clients
subsystems.policy: Python owns annotation analysis; rendering consumes prevalidated tuples and adds no request-time work. OpenAPI refuses unsupported annotations instead of publishing an empty schema. Field metadata, query bounds, primary/additional responses, deprecation, visibility and explicitly registered security schemes render from the same route image. compare_openapi reports stable breaking request/response changes. Docs endpoints are opt-in via enable_docs().

subsystems.name: configuration
subsystems.capability: Environment-driven settings with types and required-variable checks, kept separate from runtime state
subsystems.policy: Environment is an immutable string snapshot. Environment.bind constructs an ordinary dataclass once at startup, converts supported stdlib/enums/literals/unions/containers, recurses into nested groups using double-underscore keys, and raises one SettingsError containing every missing or invalid key. Env supplies an absolute alias, Secret redacts implicit formatting, and source() reports the winning process or dotenv source.

subsystems.name: middleware
subsystems.capability: Native deny-by-default known-AI-scraper policy with matching robots declarations, replaceable explicit allowances, native refusal metrics and structured Flight/OTLP dispositions; plus rate limiting and metered quotas, declarative client-fact traffic classes, CORS, CSRF, sessions, security headers, compression, request IDs, idempotency keys, and cache-control policy
subsystems.policy: `AIScrapingPolicy` is installed by a bare `Wreath()` and rejects the bundled autonomous AI scraper vocabulary after proxy/host handling but before routing; `Wreath(ai_scraping="allow")` is the explicit all-scraper opt-in, while a named allowance admits selected product tokens and refuses the remainder. User-triggered `ChatGPT-User`, `Claude-User`, and `Perplexity-User` fetches are deliberately outside the scraper set. Its native descriptor carries the operation-owned WUA database and a packed sorted rule-id table, so native ingress scans once and materializes no `Request` or Python facts. `TrafficPolicy` resolves the existing `ClientFactsProvider` once after trusted proxy handling and before rate limiting, selects the first matching bounded declaration, and publishes its name to `traffic_class(request)`, Cedar `context.client_class`, aggregate metrics, and rate-tier callbacks; unverified User-Agent and GeoIP evidence may shape traffic but are never identity. Hooks are fused into a linear tape; global middleware (`global_scope = True`) runs around routing and every response, including misses and error responses, so its `after` still runs when a handler raises. Idempotency is *response replay*, not the effect-once guarantee: `IdempotencyPolicy`'s claim must be atomic (`MemoryIdempotencyStore` is sync between read and write; `PostgresIdempotencyStore` is one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... RETURNING, where a returned row *is* the claim -- no owner column). The default store is per-worker, so the durable guarantee has to come from a unique index on the key (`jobs.enqueue(key=...)`, a unique column); design so that losing the store costs work, never correctness. `docs/cookbook/recipes/exactly-once.md` and `tests/test_exactly_once.py` hold that composition. Rate limiting has two shapes for one reason: `request.identity` is set during route authorization, so a limiter keyed on the principal cannot be a global hook. `RateLimitPolicy` stays global and keyed on the address (ingress: 404 floods, login floods) and *raises at construction* if handed `principal_key`, because degrading silently to one shared bucket is a production incident. `TieredRateLimitPolicy` is route middleware (`global_scope = False`), keyed on the principal, with one store per tier so a promotion gets a full allowance; the tier comes from the caller's roles -- the same roles Cedar authorizes with -- and the most generous match wins. The claim, the lazy statement preparation, the `clock_timestamp()` clock and the offered-not-applied schema live once, in `wreath.store`; a returned row *is* the claim, and `live`/`expired` are exact complements so a purge can never drop a row a read would still honour. `MemoryRateLimitStore` stays outside it deliberately: a token bucket is arithmetic every read advances, not a stored payload. `PostgresSessionStore.delete_for` is the only method that reads inside a session payload, so it is the only one that has to know which key holds the principal: `session_key=` at construction, overridable per call, bound as `$2::text` rather than interpolated so one prepared statement serves every key and an application string never reaches SQL. It was hardcoded to `principal`, so a deployment on `user_router(session_key=...)` got a password reset that matched no row, ended no sessions, and reported success. A **quota** is not a second limiter: `wreath.quota` declares an allowance and `RateLimitPolicy(quota=...)` charges it inside the hook that already decides the rate, because two independent limiters on one request is how a 429 comes back contradicting a 402. The rate limit is checked *first* -- a throttled request did no work, so charging it would put rejected requests on an invoice, and the meter is the one signal that cannot be sampled. Metering needs a principal, so the global form raises at construction when handed a quota, for the same reason it refuses `principal_key`. The period index is part of the counter key and lives in exactly one place (`QuotaMeter.key`), so a rollover needs no sweep and neither store re-derives it; `MemoryQuotaStore` is per-worker and says so, `PostgresQuotaStore` makes check-and-count one `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` whose row lock serializes workers. Exhaustion refuses in the tape; *degradation* is a declared state resolved into `context.quota` on the `SetFact` machinery -- and it is the one set fact **never** bounded by a delegation's `Limits`, because it is read to forbid and subtracting a forbid would let composition grant. `rows_affected` is the one reader of a PostgreSQL command tag, where there were four. The count is the **last** whitespace field, never the second: `INSERT 0 5` puts a legacy OID first, and the two readers that took the second field returned None for every insert -- indistinguishable at the call site from 'this backend does not report a count'. None rather than 0 when unreadable, because 'no rows matched' and 'this backend does not say' are different facts and recording the first when it meant the second reports a clean sweep that never happened. `wreath.log` builds on it and *raises* instead, because on a batched append 'the batch landed' must be a fact the server reported.

subsystems.name: auth
subsystems.capability: Authentication (JWT, API keys, OAuth2 and OIDC login) and authorization on a built-in Cedar policy engine
subsystems.policy: Authentication (identity) and authorization (roles, permissions, Cedar) stay firmly apart. Step-up is the one thing that spans them and lives on the authentication side: `AuthRequirement.second_factor` is a *window*, not a flag, `wreath.auth.second_factor(max_age=...)` sets it, `requirements.second_factor_age` reads `Identity.claims['second_factor_at']` and returns None (a refusal, never a zero) when there is no stamp, merging takes the strictest window, and the Cedar context omits `second_factor_age` entirely rather than faking one so `when`/`has` and `unless`/`has` policies both fail closed. The Cedar engine is built in and dependency-free: policies parse and compile in Python at startup, the per-request evaluator is C, forbid overrides permit, default deny. `permissions_router(app)` answers what the caller may do from the *same* authorizer that enforces it, and `declared_actions(app)` reads the vocabulary off the routes' `@authorize` declarations -- there is no second list to drift, and an undeclared action is refused rather than evaluated (otherwise the endpoint is an oracle for probing policies). Two questions, two shapes: the manifest is resource-type level and ETagged (the tag covers principal, roles, and the policy set, so a promotion or a deploy invalidates it and nothing else does); the batch endpoint is row level, because a Cedar decision depends on the resource. Neither is enforcement -- the route is re-evaluated on the next request, so a stale answer can only draw a button that then 403s. The vocabulary reaches the generated TS client through `ApiModel.permissions`. The permission change stream (`_livedoc.LiveDocument`, transported by `_busbridge`) is **at-most-once and advisory**: a narrowing change may arrive late, which is safe only because the manifest is for chrome and enforcement is re-evaluated on the route -- a stale manifest can draw a button that then 403s and can never permit anything. A stream never emits an ETag it cannot state truthfully: on a roles change the captured identity is stale by definition, so it emits `etag: null` rather than a tag that would tell the client to skip exactly the refetch it needs, and coalescing two pending changes lets *unknown* win. Subscriptions are capped per principal and overall and **refused** (503, client falls back to If-None-Match) rather than evicted, since evicting the oldest tab invites a reconnect that evicts the next; the ORM write subscription is registered on the first subscriber and dropped on the last, so the process-global listener list is bounded by live streams. All three discovered OIDC endpoints are pinned to the issuer origin. `jwks_uri` and `token_endpoint` go through `_same_origin_path`, which reduces them to the path their origin-pinned client takes; `authorization_endpoint` is a **browser redirect target**, so it goes through `_require_same_origin` -- the same comparison, returning the URL unchanged -- inside `discover()`, and stays absolute. Reducing it to a path would send every sign-in to this application's own `/authorize`. The check is at discovery rather than at the redirect because the attribute is public and any application may build its own redirect from it; a second check at the use site could never fire and would be a check with nothing to check. `src/wreath/_native/curves.c` is the authoritative edwards25519 and P-256 library for the whole tree; `wreath._curves` is its tuple-shaped Python facade. Field and scalar arithmetic use fixed limbs: 5x51 and 4x64 on compilers with 128-bit products, with a portable 8x32 Montgomery arm for other toolchains. Verification uses signed-window multiplication on public values. Signing and ECDH use fixed iteration counts and mask selection, so a nonce or private scalar does not steer control flow or memory indexing. RFC 6979/8032 vectors and the independent `cryptography` test dependency pin the accepted and rejected results. `context.quota` is the sixth `SetFact` and the only one whose members are restrictions rather than grants: `_resolve_quota` deliberately does not call `Limits.bound`, because intersecting a forbid-shaped fact subtracts it, and a delegated agent that could narrow `read_only` away would have used composition to gain a permission its delegator lacks.

subsystems.name: users
subsystems.capability: Registration, password and first-factor WebAuthn passkey login, email verification, password reset, scrypt password hashing, and second factors: TOTP with hashed recovery codes and WebAuthn passkeys
subsystems.policy: Second factors, stages one and two of docs/plans/second-factors-totp-webauthn.md: a TOTP code that verified once never verifies again (verify_totp requires a counter strictly greater than the credential's stored one, and SecondFactorStore.touch is an atomic conditional advance that reports whether it won -- one statement with WHERE counter < $1 in OrmSecondFactorStore, a compare-and-set in a synchronous function in InMemorySecondFactorStore -- so a lost advance is refused as a replay and two concurrent requests carrying one code cannot both complete); skew is one step by default and never more than _secondfactor.MAX_SKEW; enrolment is two-phase, so begin_totp_enrolment writes nothing and only a verified code creates a credential, and the unconfirmed secret lives in the `enrolments` SessionStore under an opaque id when one is passed, bound to the user who began it; recovery codes are a single SHA-256 (hash_recovery_code) rather than the password hasher -- ~78 bits needs no slow KDF, passwords still get scrypt -- shown once, compared with hmac.compare_digest, and deleted when redeemed -- the deletion claimed through the same conditional advance the TOTP branch uses, since a remove() that returns nothing cannot say which of two simultaneous redemptions spent the code, with stage one's scrypt$ rows still verifying; a login awaiting a second factor writes a pending marker and never a principal, so SessionIdentityBackend yields no identity for it; verification (promotion or step-up) rotates the session and stamps second_factor_at, which AuthRequirement.second_factor / wreath.auth.second_factor and the Cedar context's second_factor_age read, absent always meaning refused rather than fresh; DELETE /auth/2fa/{id} needs a factor within step_up_ttl, is owner-scoped, refuses a recovery id, and takes the recovery codes with the last real factor; the credential material column is named secret_material because crud.SENSITIVE_FIELD matches that and not `material`. Stage three adds WebAuthn as a second factor, all Python and no new C: _webauthn.py parses CBOR/COSE/authenticator data/DER and delegates every signature to _auth/_ecverify (ES256 and Ed25519 only -- RS256 is refused by name rather than implemented), the parsers refuse indefinite-length CBOR, tags, floats, duplicate keys, trailing bytes, non-minimal DER integers and off-curve points, and only `none` attestation is accepted because verifying an attestation statement needs a metadata service; a ceremony's type, challenge, origin and RP ID hash are four separate refusals; the challenge lives in a ChallengeStore (wreath.store's Keyed primitive, MemoryChallengeStore by default and PostgresChallengeStore for a fleet) rather than in the session, and is spent by one DELETE ... WHERE handle AND user_id AND kind AND expires > clock_timestamp() RETURNING payload -- so the returned row *is* the consumption (two concurrent completions cannot both proceed) and the user binding is a WHERE clause rather than a check after the row is already gone (a mismatched attempt matches no row, deletes nothing, and costs the rightful user nothing). The candidate subject is derived from the session -- a pending login first, then the signed-in principal -- and passed to that statement as a precondition, never read back out of the record, because a record that names its own owner lets whoever holds a handle define who they are; ChallengeStore.peek is a non-consuming read used by the TOTP enrolment path (whose property is confirmed-exactly-once, not read-exactly-once: a mistyped code must not cost a fresh QR scan) and, after a consume has already refused, to choose between ceremony_expired and the binding refusal -- it applies no binding and no security decision rests on it; a signature counter that fails to increase above a stored non-zero one is refused as a clone signal while an authenticator that always reports 0 keeps working; user verification is requested (not required) and its outcome is recorded on the session as second_factor_uv; the webauthn routes mount only when second_factor_router is given rp_id. The accepted origins default to https://{rp_id} and widen for exactly one case: _webauthn.default_origins admits http:// as well when rp_id is a loopback host (localhost, ::1, 127.0.0.0/8), and _webauthn.origin_accepted lets a loopback origin carry any port, since http://localhost:8000 is a secure context and no default set can enumerate a development port -- no other host is ever admitted over http, no port is tolerated off loopback, and there is no wildcard. Building second_factor_router without enrolments= no longer warns, because it no longer degrades: ceremony state goes to a ChallengeStore whose default is real, so the single-use property holds unconditionally instead of being announced as absent. The removed UserWarning could only ever name half its condition -- a router built before any application exists cannot observe whether SessionPolicy was given a store= -- and a warning nobody can act on with certainty is one people learn to ignore. One behaviour change comes with it, for multi-worker deployments on cookie sessions with no store named: a ceremony is now confined to the worker that began it, which fails closed (refused, begin again) and is what challenges=PostgresChallengeStore answers. The webauthn suite's authenticator is synthetic (a real key and a real signature from cryptography, a dev/test dependency), which proves agreement about the wire formats and not interoperability; interoperability is pinned by one recorded registration and one recorded assertion transcribed from the W3C WebAuthn Level 3 specification's own section 16.2 test vectors (CR Snapshot, 26 May 2026), cited in place -- do not replace those with generated bytes. The two routers are separate but not independent: second_factor_router records itself against the UserStore it was built with, so a user_router over that same store with no second_factors= of its own refuses (500 second_factor_not_wired, no session written) the login of a user who has a non-recovery factor, rather than issuing a password-only sign-in -- and the same refusal covers the other half-wiring, a user_router given a SecondFactorStore that is not the object second_factor_router writes to, which otherwise read an empty store and signed the caller in; and user_router's login and logout both clear pending_totp_enrolment and pending_webauthn from the session and delete the rows behind them, so a ceremony does not outlive the sitting it began in. Every one of those checks is a raise, never an assert. `user_router` hands its own `session_key` to `sessions.delete_for` when it is not the default, so a password reset enumerates by the key login actually wrote the principal under; the default call shape is unchanged so a store written against the one-argument signature keeps working.

subsystems.name: sso
subsystems.capability: SAML and OIDC login flows over the assertion verification wreath already owned, including per-organisation identity-provider metadata and SAML request/response routing
subsystems.policy: The flows, never a second verifier: `SamlServiceProvider.consume` builds the `IdentityProvider`/`ServiceProvider`/`in_response_to` that `saml.verify_response` already takes. **The trust anchor is per organisation and comes from the login that began**, never from the assertion -- verifying against the union of every configured certificate lets one customer's identity provider mint an identity in another's, with no signature check failing anywhere, and reading the organisation out of the assertion is the same defect one indirection along. `PendingLogin` carries it and is single-use, so an assertion answering no request is unsolicited rather than a login as anybody from a captured POST body. Attribute mapping is declared and an undeclared attribute is refused: a heuristic that reads `email` and misses `mail` is confident, wrong, and produces one duplicate account per user per provider. JIT provisioning creates account and membership together, adopts an existing account rather than duplicating it (the choice `scim_router` already makes), refuses a role outside the declared vocabulary at *configuration* time because an IdP attribute is whatever a customer's directory admin typed, and yields a **pending** session where the organisation requires a second factor so it composes with `SessionIdentityBackend` rather than bypassing it. OIDC requires S256 PKCE (`plain` sends the verifier as the challenge), binds state to the session that began the flow (an attacker's code redeemed in a victim's browser signs them into the attacker's account) and checks the id token's nonce. **Nothing is fetched on the request path** -- discovery and JWKS refresh at startup, and an unknown `kid` is simply unverified -- the rule `wreath.signatures` already holds, because a request-driven fetch lets an unauthenticated caller aim an outbound request.

subsystems.name: oauth
subsystems.capability: An OAuth 2.1 authorization server for a deployment that issues its own tokens, minting exactly what wreath already verifies
subsystems.policy: The first obligation is that what it mints is what `JwtVerifier` and `MCPAuth` verify; an issuer whose output its own verifier rejects is two features rather than one, so the tests drive a minted token through the real verifier. Signing is HS256 over the stdlib, keeping the no-mandatory-dependency rule -- right for an issuer that is also the resource server, wrong for one whose tokens third parties verify, and `jwks()` returning an empty key set says so rather than emitting the shared secret as an `oct` entry. Three replay defences, separate because they fail differently: an authorization code is single-use and a second redemption **revokes the token the first issued** (refusing only the second leaves the attacker's token live if they got there first); a refresh token rotates and reuse revokes the whole chain, since rotation without reuse detection tells you nothing; PKCE is required and `plain` refused. A redirect URI is matched **exactly** -- `https://app.example.evil/cb` has the registered URI as a prefix, and an open redirect on the authorization endpoint is a code exfiltration. Client credentials carry no subject, because a machine token naming a person is a machine that can act as one, and a public client cannot use the grant at all. A token carries its tenant, so it composes with `wreath.tenancy` rather than around it.

subsystems.name: organizations
subsystems.capability: Tenancy at the identity layer: durable organisations, memberships, roles within them, single-use invitations that survive both the invitee having no account and API restarts, the composed principal every authorization fact hangs off, and SCIM 2.0 provisioning with filtering, sorting and paging as an adapter onto exactly those stores
subsystems.policy: Composition never grants. `Limits` and `Narrowing` can only reduce what a principal may do: a limit is intersected with what a provider resolved, and `Principal.narrow` has the delegating principal's own decision evaluated as a conjunct by `CedarAuthorizer`, so permitted(narrow(P, N)) is a subset of permitted(P) for every policy set -- including ones that permit only delegates. That is a property test over generated policy sets (tests/test_principal_narrow.py), falsified by injecting a union. Delegation scope and expiry are enforced mechanically before the engine is consulted, never as a policy-readable key, so a permissive policy set cannot widen them. Roles are namespaced '<org>:<role>' on the way into context and never stored that way; unqualified roles come only from the active organisation, so a policy written without thinking about tenancy is still tenant-safe. Every set-valued Cedar context key is one `SetFact`: resolved once per request, resolved at all only when a policy names it, empty-and-supplied when no provider is configured (an absent key skips an `unless` forbid rather than standing it), and refused at startup when a policy names something the provider does not hold -- except organisation ids, which are rows rather than configuration and must not stop the process booting. Membership resolution is synchronous by design: `Memberships` reads a snapshot loaded where identity was established, so authorization never opens a connection. SCIM 2.0 (`scim_router`, RFC 7643 and 7644) is an adapter and owns no data: a SCIM User is a `wreath.users` record, a SCIM Group *is* a role in the store's declared vocabulary, and membership is this module's `Membership` -- so what a directory writes is the row `context.organizations` and `context.org_roles` read. There is no allow/deny decision in `_scim`: every route carries `@authorize(action=scim_read|scim_write, resource='Organization::"<org>"')` answered by the application's own authorizer, and the router **refuses to build** when none is configured (decision 0019). The two de-provisioning verbs differ on purpose and reversing either loses data: DELETE removes the *membership* and never cascades to content, while `active: false` disables the *account* and is refused with `mutability` when the user is a member of another organisation, because `UserRecord.is_active` is not tenant-scoped. POST /Users adopts an existing account rather than minting a second one for an email; removing an absent group member is a no-op so a retried de-provisioning converges, while a `replace` through a filter matching nothing is `noTarget` as the RFC requires. Groups cannot be created or deleted (501) and `displayName` is immutable, because the role vocabulary is configuration a Cedar policy names by string. A filter naming an attribute wreath does not store -- externalId, name.* -- is 400 `invalidFilter`, never an empty page, since an empty page is what makes a directory recreate everyone; `/Schemas` publishes only what is stored. Filter length, depth and the members one filtered request may scan are bounded. `PATCH` and `PUT` are pure functions producing the next representation (`_scim/patch.py`) and one writer reconciles it, so the two verbs cannot disagree about what an attribute means. Listing an organisation's members is the separate `MemberDirectory` seam, because authorization never asks that question and a store that only backs authorization need not answer it.

subsystems.name: postgres
subsystems.capability: A native PostgreSQL driver: connection pooling, prepared statements, and parameter type inference
subsystems.policy: Connection.map/Statement.map run one Sync-delimited operation per input in input order (no coalescing/dedup); Connection.transaction() orders reads before dependent writes and discards a connection whose synchronization cannot be proven.

subsystems.name: locks
subsystems.capability: Cluster-wide mutexes and run-once leases, on PostgreSQL advisory locks rather than a second datastore
subsystems.policy: Advisory locks and SingletonRunner are reached through the wreath.postgres facade, not imported from _locks directly.

subsystems.name: orm
subsystems.capability: An async ORM with explicit loading, first-class JSONB and array columns, vector similarity and full-text search without a second datastore, transactions, and tenant-scoped sessions
subsystems.policy:
The dependency direction is one-way: wreath.orm imports wreath.postgres, never the reverse. Attribute access never performs I/O; loading is explicit (no lazy N+1). Generated per-model C layouts are authoritative: scalar cells are inline, state is held in bitmaps, complete constructor keyword sets are preflighted and filled in one native loop, and Python resolves only omitted defaults and cross-field rules. The immutable versioned model API is passed into bulk core operations per call. the query cache-key (orm_shape) must produce bytes identical to _shape_of_walk or the plan cache splits. An extension type's OID is assigned by CREATE EXTENSION and so differs between databases: it is resolved once at startup (orm/introspection.resolve_extension_types) and must never reach a plan-cache shape token or a model fingerprint, both of which are name-derived instead. ColumnSpec.oid reads through the type rather than snapshotting it, and the model layout -- which does bake the OID in at class definition -- is written back by rebind_storage_oid at the same moment. An ORDER BY key that is not a bare column (a vector distance) takes the walked keyer deliberately, because orm_shape.c reads ordering.expression.column. A generated column (`TsVector`) is the database's to write, never the application's: its expression names other columns, so it is rendered by orm/_generated.py once the registry knows their names and types, in PostgreSQL's own deparsed normal form -- a spelling that differs by one byte reports the column as drifted on every migration run, forever.

**Wreath implements the client half of pgvector, never the server half.** The wire codec is ours -- `_pgdriver.py` and `_native/postgres/codec.c` -- so no `pgvector` Python package is needed and `replaces` lists it for that reason. The `vector`/`halfvec` *types*, the `<->`/`<=>`/`<#>`/`<+>` operators and the HNSW/IVFFlat access methods are extension code inside PostgreSQL; `CREATE EXTENSION vector` is required and no client driver can substitute for it, because an index access method cannot be defined from outside the server. Migrations deliberately never emit `CREATE EXTENSION` (the privilege is usually not the runner's) and `doctor.check_extension_types` is the pre-flight.

**`halfvec` is a second codec kind, not a variant of the first.** `EXT_KIND_VECTOR = 1` frames float4 elements and `EXT_KIND_HALFVEC = 2` frames float2; one OID must never mean two wire formats, since decoding one as the other yields a plausible vector of the wrong length. Adding a kind means a branch in *both* twins at all six dispatch sites (text/binary x encode/decode, plus the two `_decode_value` entry points) -- a missed site silently returns raw bytes, which is how this one was caught. The text form is shared: pgvector prints both types as `[1,2,3]`. Elements are bounded by binary16's largest finite value (65504, `MAX_HALF_MAGNITUDE`) at coercion *and* at encode, because a larger value rounds to an infinity pgvector then refuses. `Halfvec`'s `extension` is `"vector"`, not `"halfvec"` -- one extension provides both, and naming the type would send readers to install something nonexistent. Operator classes are per type (`halfvec_cosine_ops`).

**`sparsevec` is a third kind (`EXT_KIND_SPARSEVEC = 3`) and `bit` is not an extension type at all.** The same six-dispatch-site rule applies to `sparsevec`, plus a seventh consideration the first two did not have: its Python value is neither a list nor anything else a builtin can express, so `wreath._sparsevec.SparseVector` carries the dimension and the index-to-value mapping together. That module holds one class and imports nothing from wreath, because both halves of the driver need it -- `_pgdriver.py` imports it directly and `codec.c` resolves it in module init beside `uuid.UUID`. Its validation is not restated in C: two copies of a bounds check are two chances to disagree about what pgvector accepts, and the sparse paths are cold. **`SparseVector` counts indices from 1** (pgvector's text form and its documentation do) while the binary wire counts from 0; the conversion lives in `_encode_sparsevec`/`_decode_sparsevec` and their C twins and nowhere else. It carries `_pg_oid` on a *copy* made by `to_wire`, for the same parameter-inference reason `WireList` exists, because the caller's own value may outlive the bind and be bound against another database.

**`Bit` is PostgreSQL's own `bit`, OID 1560 -- a compile-time constant with no resolution step.** Only pgvector's `<~>` (hamming) and `<%>` (jaccard) operators over it, and the `bit_hamming_ops`/`bit_jaccard_ops` index classes, come from the extension, which is why `_bit_distance` gates on the OID rather than on `isinstance(pg_type, ExtensionType)`. The wire format packs bits MSB-first with the final byte padded on the right; reversed, every value still round-trips through the codec and every distance the server computes is wrong, so `tests/orm/test_bit_codec.py` asserts the packing against literal bytes rather than only through a round trip. Non-zero padding is refused rather than masked away, because masking would make two wire values decode to one string.

**A halfvec value's decimal depends on the result format**: the binary decoder widens the stored binary16 exactly (`0.0999755859375`), pgvector's text rendering prints nine significant digits (`0.099975586`). Different Python floats. Pinned in `tests/orm/test_halfvec_live.py`.

subsystems.name: series
subsystems.capability: Chart data as a declaration or storage-neutral native data kernel: DST-correct buckets, fills, downsampling, paths, and axes
subsystems.policy: Chart data as a declaration over one source model, with a bounded result. Bucketing is a timezone problem before it is an aggregation problem: the bucket is assigned and the spine generated on the local wall clock, then converted back, because generate_series stepping naive timestamps advances a calendar day while stepping timestamptz advances exactly 24 hours -- the DST bug, twice a year, in one bucket. Ranges are half-open and stated once, for the filter and the spine bounds alike. Fill is per measure: count and sum fill with 0, avg/min/max stay null, because an average of no rows is undefined and drawing it as zero reads as a collapse rather than an absence. A series is identified by a stable key from the grouping value, never by rank, so a filter change cannot repaint a legend. Multiple measures are multiple named series and are never merged -- two units on one pair of axes is a dual-axis chart, whose alignment is arbitrary. Top-N folds (it preserves the total) and the fold is applied before aggregation, so the remainder's average is a real average and not an average of averages; every other ceiling refuses rather than truncating. Not plan-cached, following compile_count: a declaration runs once per chart request, not once per row. Bucket vocabulary lives in wreath.temporal because sealing will need end_of() too.

subsystems.name: infra
subsystems.capability: Infrastructure inferred from an application's own declarations, plus a checksummed provider-neutral Compose bundle for an immutable OCI image
subsystems.policy: Stage 1 is read-only: `wreath infra infer` derives a typed plan from the objects an application's declarations built, and never imports a cloud SDK, opens a socket, writes state, or applies anything -- both properties are asserted by tests. Inference walks the registries itself rather than calling Wreath._components_by_database, because that lookup misses JobRunner._db and a middleware's _store. A settings dataclass named with --settings is turned into the keys Environment.bind will read and checked against --env/--environ; a required key with no supplier is a gap and the command exits 1. Subsystems needing no new infrastructure are listed as such, including the ones the application does not use, because the absence of a broker is the finding. `wreath infra bundle` accepts only a gap-free plan and immutable OCI image digest, then writes Compose, the original plan, a machine-readable deployment contract, and checksums without building, pulling, provisioning, or applying. Provider declarations, Terraform/OpenTofu output, live diff, state, and apply are not shipped.

subsystems.name: migrations
subsystems.capability: Schema diffing, migration artifacts, apply, and a derived inverse that refuses to strand live code
subsystems.policy: Readiness resolution is metal-only. The inverse `down` is derived from the same artifact as the forward migration and refuses to strand live ORM code unless --force. Single-schema `apply` and tenant-fleet `apply_fleet` both ship; the fleet form applies one artifact serially under a session advisory lock and one transaction per tenant. A deferred migration declares its conversion beside the model rather than in a migration file, because artifacts are generated from the catalog and there is nothing to decorate. `Recode` (same type, new values) is guarded by a predicate scan that refuses ordered comparison, patterns, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY` and joins on a converting column; `Retype` (new type, two columns) is guarded by the gate instead, because an unconverted row reads NULL rather than reading wrong. Refusal is the default: a false refusal costs an argument, a false permission costs a silent incident. A scan that examined nothing refuses rather than reporting clean. **A column's SQL type is reconstructed from its OID, and two kinds of type cannot be.** `migration_sql.c::sql_type_for_oid` maps a built-in OID to its spelling and a type missing from that switch does not fail loudly: it renders as an *empty* `MANUAL` statement, so `generate` omits the column and then emits the constraints and indexes that reference it, and applying the plan fails on a column that was never added. `json`, `character varying` and `bit(n)` were all missing this way, which is why tests/migrations/test_object_coverage.py now enumerates every built-in `PgType` in `__all__` rather than the ones somebody thought of. The second kind is a type whose *modifier* is part of it: `bit(8)` and `bit(512)` share OID 1560, so the OID alone loses the width. Those spell themselves in the descriptor exactly as an extension type does, and the set is written twice -- `migrations._MODIFIER_BEARING_OIDS` and a hard-coded `<> 1560` in `_SINGLE_CATALOG_SQL`, because a CASE cannot read a frozenset. **Both sides must produce the identical string or the column is rediscovered as drift on every run forever**, which is the same silent failure the vector default-opclass defect had; test_catalog_integration.py holds them equal against a real catalog. `apply_fleet` runs one artifact across many tenant schemas: a session advisory lock (two deploys interleaving per-tenant transactions would leave a fleet in a state neither artifact describes, and `pg_try_advisory_lock` refuses a second runner rather than queueing behind a run that may take an hour), one transaction per tenant because one spanning a thousand schemas holds every lock for the length of the slowest, a tenant already at the target skipped rather than refused so a stopped run is finished by re-running, and serial application because concurrent DDL contends on shared catalog rows and the failure it produces is a deadlock partway through a fleet. Every tenant goes through the *same* `_apply_artifact_to_schema` as a single-schema run -- the five refusals are the whole safety argument of a migration and a fleet-only copy is exactly where a drift would go unnoticed, being the path nobody runs by hand. **A fleet is blocked on fingerprints, not on the loop**: `nspname` is the first column of every catalog branch, so byte-identical tenants fingerprint differently. `_FLEET_CATALOG_SQL` blanks tenant-local names while keeping a foreign key into a shared schema named -- a fact every tenant shares rather than a difference -- and `generate_single_plan(fleet=True)` reads through it. The desired image and the DDL are still schema-qualified; both want the fleet desired-image compiler, which `_registry_descriptor` already refuses an unqualified spec by name for. A fleet artifact is produced by `generate_single_plan(fleet=True)` and crosses every structurally identical tenant. Three things embedded the schema name and all three are neutralised: the catalog fingerprint (`_FLEET_CATALOG_SQL` blanks tenant-local names, keeping a foreign key into a *shared* schema named because that is a fact every tenant shares rather than a difference), the desired image (`_registry_descriptor(fleet=True)` writes each spec's schema empty), and the DDL (a zero-length schema renders unqualified). **A zero-length schema therefore means tenant template rather than malformed**, and the three native parsers that refused it were changed to say so; the table name stays required, because an operation naming no relation is a corrupt tape however it was produced. `apply_fleet` binds `SET LOCAL search_path` per tenant so unqualified DDL lands in the right schema -- transaction-local, so it cannot leak onto a pooled connection's next borrower.

subsystems.name: tenancy
subsystems.capability: Tenant isolation PostgreSQL enforces: a role and a grant set per tenant, a directory to resolve one from a request, and a central schema every tenant reads and none may write
subsystems.policy: `search_path` is ergonomics; the role is the boundary. A search path decides where an *unqualified* name resolves and one qualified identifier walks past it, so isolation by naming cannot be audited -- the thing to audit would be every query ever written. A tenant role holds privileges on its own schema plus SELECT on the central schema and nothing on any other tenant's, so a cross-tenant read is `permission denied` from the server and the audit is a catalog query (`isolation_report`). The application's login role is NOINHERIT and holds membership without inheritance, which is what makes RESET ROLE a dead end rather than an escape hatch; `verify_isolation` refuses a superuser, an inheriting role, or a role that owns tenant schemas, at startup, because none of those can be compensated for by any grant set. Three residuals are stated rather than papered over: a deliberate `SET ROLE other_tenant` still crosses (membership is what lets the pool switch at all), and table *names* leak because pg_catalog is world-readable -- revoking USAGE stops reaching an object, not seeing it exists. `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` is what stops the grants drifting as migrations add tables. Resolution is two halves on purpose: a source *names* a tenant, a directory *finds* it -- a header used directly as a schema is a header that can name any schema. `FromORM(tenant=FromTenant())` is the load-bearing seam: before it the only tenant-bound session was hand-built in a handler body, so the declarative spelling produced an unbound session and the safe path was the one you had to remember. An isolated registry bound without a tenant is refused at route-compile time.

subsystems.name: jobs
subsystems.capability: Durable Postgres-backed jobs and schedules, pub/sub messaging, WebSocket rooms, task progress, and supervised background services
subsystems.policy: PostgreSQL is the queue; there is no broker to operate. The service supervisor starts after databases and before user startup handlers, and stops in reverse: stop fetching, drain bounded in-flight work, then cancel. Watchable work: `JobRunner(progress=ProgressRegistry(...))` makes the job id the task id -- one identifier, no correlation -- and `launch()` seeds it `queued` so a client polling before a worker claims it does not get a 404. The runner owns the terminal states because only it can tell a retry from a dead-letter: success reports `done`, dead-letter reports `failed` with the error, and a retry leaves the task `running`. A handler never reports terminal state itself. `ProgressRegistry(bus)` carries reports to every worker on one channel with the rooms.py origin guard (apply locally, publish once, never relay what arrived); at-most-once, and a bus failure cannot fail the work being reported on. Cross-worker transport discipline is one primitive: `_busbridge.BusBridge` owns the channel, the origin tag that drops a worker's own NOTIFY echo, and the deferred publish, and there is deliberately **no path from its receive to a publish** -- never-relaying is structural, not a flag. `rooms.py`, `progress.py`, and `_orm_events.WriteBroadcast` each keep only their payload shape and local apply. The one real difference is preserved: rooms publishes inline and unsuppressed (its caller is awaiting the fan-out), the other two are fire-and-forget and swallow (the row already committed; a percentage is commentary). Durable subscriber groups are discovered fleet-wide from a `message_groups` table, **unioned** with local registrations so a missing table degrades to the old behaviour and shipping before the DDL cannot regress; the snapshot is refreshed on a timer (`group_refresh`, 30s) rather than read per publish, because a query inside the caller's `tx` would abort *their* transaction if the table were absent. Registry failures are counted (`group_registry_errors`), never raised. A publish routed to nobody stays a no-op but increments `unrouted_publishes`; `require_group=True` raises `NoSubscriberGroup` instead. The doorbell's held LISTEN connection is supervised: it reconnects with jittered exponential backoff (50 ms to 5 s, no reset for a connection that flaps), counts losses and failed opens in `doorbell_reconnects`, and counts ephemeral handler exceptions separately in `handler_errors` so a bug in user code cannot read as a dropped connection. A handler is cancelled at `deadline_for(task)` -- `task(timeout=...)`, defaulting to `DEADLINE_FRACTION` (0.8) of the lease, and refused at registration if it is not shorter than the lease. There is no heartbeat, so a handler still running when its lease expires is reclaimed and run again by another worker: the fence stops the loser's bookkeeping landing, never the duplicate side effect. `drive()` passes a pass's own `shift` as its deadline rather than taking the default, because that bound is already declared and already checked. A cancelled handler charges an attempt and retries (a deadline miss is usually a slow dependency) and counts in `run_timeouts`, apart from `run_errors`: nothing failed, work was stopped. Claim order is `priority DESC, run_at` and the partial index leads with it -- replaced rather than added beside the old `(queue, run_at)` one, which could not serve the new ordering. `priority` is defaulted rather than nullable because ORDER BY DESC sorts NULL first, so an older build's rows would outrank everything the moment the step landed. It is a lane and not a promise: a strict priority queue starves its low lane by definition and sizing for that stays the caller's. `enqueue(coalesce=True)` merges onto a repeated key instead of dropping -- newest args, earliest run_at via LEAST, highest priority via GREATEST, all in the one statement because a read-then-write lets two callers interleave and lose an update -- and only `WHERE state = 'ready'`, since rewriting a leased job's arguments would hand its worker inputs it never read. It refuses without a key: there is nothing to coalesce onto, and a silent no-op would read as a merge. `owner` on a claimed row is a per-process identity (`{queue}:{12 hex}`), not the queue name it used to be -- every worker on a queue shared one, so the column answered a question the `queue` column already answers and nothing read it back. Correctness never depended on it and still does not (the fence is what stops a superseded worker's bookkeeping landing); what it buys is naming the process that holds a job during an incident. Generated rather than derived from a host name or pid, both of which repeat across containers and restarts. Column presence is one cached probe (`_carries`) over `_pgcatalog.column_exists`, not a hand-rolled catalog query per column. The **default enqueue never names `priority` and therefore never probes for it**: the column has a server-side DEFAULT so omitting it writes the same row, and a probe on the common path would put a catalog read on an enqueue with no use for the answer. A caller that asks for an ordering against a schema without the column is refused by name rather than silently unprioritised. The claim's ORDER BY degrades to `run_at` when the column is absent, resolved at `start` so the claim loop never asks.

subsystems.name: workflows
subsystems.capability: Durable multi-step sagas: ordered steps whose results are recorded before the next starts, resume from the first unrecorded step, and compensation newest-first when one raises
subsystems.policy:
**A completed step never runs twice.** Each step's return value is recorded before the next one starts, so `resume` re-enters at the first step with no record and reads the *recorded* result rather than recomputing it. That is the whole difference from a loop over callables.

**Compensation runs newest-first, and the step that raised is not compensated** -- it never completed, so there is nothing of its to undo, and an undo against state that was never established turns a recoverable failure into a corrupt one.

**A compensation that raises is counted, not swallowed** (AGENTS.md's third tier: broad catch, counted, waived in place with a reason). The undos behind a failed one still run, or the saga is left more broken than if nothing had been undone. The count is durable on the instance and read with `Workflow.status`, because a run that compensates re-raises the step's own exception -- so the summary cannot come back as a return value, and a half-compensated saga has to be findable later by someone without the traceback.

**Renaming a step of a live instance raises `WorkflowDefinitionChanged`.** Completion is keyed on the step *name*, so a rename leaves a record matching nothing and a naive resume redoes completed work and reports success. The stored step list is written at `begin` for exactly this comparison. This is the one failure here that would otherwise be invisible.

`PostgresWorkflowStore` keeps its two tables in a dedicated system schema with a `tenant` column and never relies on `search_path`, which is `jobs`'s rule for the same reason. Its resume path is covered against a live server by `tests/test_workflows_checklist.py::test_postgres_store_survives_a_crash_between_steps` (marked `network`, gated on `WREATH_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN`), because the in-memory store satisfies the resume contract only within one process -- precisely not the situation sagas exist for. A step can be **recorded**: `Workflow.run(recorder=WorkflowStepRecorder(...))` writes a `WFST` record into the same `WFR1` container `ATMP` goes into -- a second record kind, never a second format. The unit genuinely differs from a job attempt, which is why it is a kind rather than a rename: identity is `(instance, step)` with a *position* and no fence, cause is the step before it rather than the request that enqueued it, and the record carries the undo chain newest-first as `(step, ran|failed|none)` -- `none` being a third answer because "nothing to undo" and "the undo was never reached" are different states. It is written **after** the compensations run, since a record written at the raise could carry none of them. Three outcomes: `completed`, `raised` (stopped and unwound cleanly, re-runnable) and `compensation_failed` (stopped and did not unwind, which no retry reaches), and the third outranks the second so a reader is not sent to the original failure. Deny-by-default with no `argument_allowlist`, because a step takes no arguments -- a `StepContext` holds application objects rather than the JSON a queue row stored -- so only the count of prior completions is recorded. Sampling is keyed on the instance, so a saga is kept or dropped whole; a per-step sample would keep step 2 and step 5 and read as a saga that skipped work. `_compensate` now returns the chain as its third value, and `_StepWitness` keeps every recording decision out of the saga: an unarmed run pays one attribute test per step.

subsystems.name: passes
subsystems.capability: Backfills, rollups, and reindexes as a durable, resumable, paced walk over a big table
subsystems.policy: A pass converts the past; the application writes the future in the shape the pass is converting to. That precondition is the primitive's rule rather than a caller's choice, and it is what makes a fixed ceiling sound. The cursor advances inside the chunk transaction, so position and data commit together -- the whole reason this is worth owning is that the ledger row and the walked table are two rows in one PostgreSQL cluster. The compare-and-swap is the chunk's first statement: it takes the row lock, so two workers serialise and the loser rolls back whole rather than doing anything observable. That exclusivity argument is why parallel sharded execution is deliberately not planned. The vocabulary is 'a half-open range over one ordered domain'; row counts are reported, never structural, so a bucketed range source still fits. Keyset never OFFSET is a complexity argument (N^2/(2c) against (N/c)*log N + N) and needs no benchmark -- its two correctness conditions are refusals: the leading key column must be indexed, and a composite key is one row comparison, never expanded ORs. A boundary that cannot be proven unique is refused because '>' silently skips siblings and '>=' loops forever. Pacing ships in the first release rather than after it: the primitive must not have a version in which an unpaced walk exists.

subsystems.name: objects
subsystems.capability: Object storage over S3-compatible services or local disk, with presigned uploads and downloads, and resumable uploads admitted at the boundary
subsystems.policy: Blob/object storage: the `ObjectStore` protocol with `MemoryObjectStore` (the dev/test twin), a symlink-safe `LocalObjectStore` on the same `openat` containment as static files, and `S3ObjectStore` over `http_client` signed with zero-dependency SigV4. `normalize_key` is the single containment gate for every backend -- a key is validated there, not per backend. Named `objects` because "store" meant two unrelated things: this, and the small keyed tables behind rate limiting, idempotency, and sessions (`wreath.store`). `src/wreath/storage.py` is a deprecating alias that re-exports the old names (`Storage`/`S3Storage`/`StoragePath`/`StorageError`) and warns; it exists so the rename cannot break an existing import, and is removable once callers have moved. **Resumable uploads live here rather than in a module of their own**, because they are a way to write an object. The shipped surface is `draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload-12` and tus 1.0.x is deliberately not served: the vocabularies overlap enough that one implementation answering both would have to guess a dialect from headers a client did not send. The trade against `url()` is the point -- a presigned URL routes around Cedar, the quota and the declared media type, and this path keeps the application in the way of those decisions while the bytes stream in restartable pieces. Upload state is a separate `UploadStore` because its lifetime is the opposite of an object's; `MemoryUploadStore` is the default and confines an upload to one worker (a resume elsewhere is a 404, which fails closed), and `ObjectUploadStore` is the shared one that needs no second datastore. `advance` is conditional and reports whether it won, so two racing appends lose one rather than punching a hole. S3 assembles with its own multipart, which is why a non-final append has a floor that `Upload-Limit: min-append-size` advertises rather than hides.

subsystems.name: grpc
subsystems.capability: Serve gRPC methods over the native HTTP/2 server, declared as routes so one authorization vocabulary covers REST and gRPC alike
subsystems.policy: A gRPC method is a *route*, registered as `POST /{service}/{method}` on an ordinary `Router`. That is not a convenience: it is what makes `@roles`, `@authorize`, `permissions=` and `dependencies=` mean the same thing here as on a REST route, enforced by the same tape and read by `permissions_router` and `wreath mutant` from the same place -- there is no second authorization model to drift. The route registers a *wrapper* around the user's function, so `GrpcService.router` copies the `AuthRequirement` the auth decorators recorded on their function onto the wrapper; without that copy a `@roles` on a gRPC method would read as enforcement and enforce nothing, which is precisely the unwatched control the mutation tester exists to find. `_GrpcResponse` subclasses `StreamingResponse` because the application's return-value coercion is a closed isinstance check over four response types -- duck-typing `__call__(send)` is not enough -- and inheriting also picks up the deferred-cleanup contract that releases a borrowed database connection. It drives `http.response.start(trailers=True)`, bodies, then `http.response.trailers` itself, which is the only path to the ASGI trailers extension: the native HTTP/2 server implements it in C and nothing else in `wreath.response` ever sends those messages. The HTTP status is always 200, including for a refusal, because in gRPC the transport succeeded whenever the server was reached and the outcome is the `grpc-status` trailer; a handler that fails after its first message is already on the wire reports its status there rather than re-raising, since re-raising aborts the stream with no status and a client reads that as an unexplained transport error instead of the refusal it was. An unrecognised exception maps to UNKNOWN and never to UNAVAILABLE or ABORTED, both of which tell a client to retry. The four-byte length prefix is attacker-controlled and is checked against `max_message_bytes` before anything is allocated. Two transport constraints come from the server and not from here: gRPC needs response trailers, which only wreath's own server emits, and wreath negotiates h2 through ALPN and never sniffs the first application bytes, so prior-knowledge h2c is unavailable and gRPC requires TLS. **ASGI offers no way to learn at startup which protocols the server will speak**, so the refusal for a foreign server is the first thing every call does rather than a startup check. Server reflection is not built and is coupled to `wreath.protobuf` deliberately not building descriptors; a gRPC *client* is not built because `http_client` has no HTTP/2 at all.

subsystems.name: mcp
subsystems.capability: A Model Context Protocol server: declared Python callables served to a model as tools, resources and prompts, over streamable HTTP
subsystems.policy: Stages 1-4 of `docs/plans/native-mcp-server.md`: `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/*`, `resources/*`, `prompts/*` and `notifications/cancelled` over streamable HTTP, the `GET` server-to-client stream, `expose_routes`, plus the whole authorization boundary. **No new C, at any stage** -- the plan decided this: the JSON-RPC envelope is `_native/json.c`, SSE framing is `_native/sse.c` via `SSEResponse`, ingress and routing are the ordinary native path, token verification rides `jose.c` through `JwtVerifier`, authorization rides `cedar.c` through `CedarAuthorizer`, and what is left is startup-time registration plus once-per-call orchestration. A tool's `inputSchema` is derived from `binding.inspect_handler` and rendered by `openapi._openapi_schema`/`_component_schema`, differing from the OpenAPI document only in the `$ref` base (`#/$defs/` against `#/components/schemas/`); `tests/test_mcp_schema.py` pins that parity and is the reason there is no second validator. The stage-1 optimization is Python and is the cached `tools/list` bytes -- `ToolRegistry.listing()` serializes once and registration invalidates it. A binding source a call cannot fill (header, cookie, form field, upload, path placeholder, `Depends`) is refused at registration, not at call time. **Five outcomes stay distinguishable**, for the reason `messaging.MessageBus` separates `doorbell_reconnects` from `handler_errors`: `ToolError` is a *result* carrying `isError`; an unplanned exception is caught at the boundary, counted in `tool_errors`, and reports only its type; arguments that miss the schema never reach the tool and count in `schema_rejections`; a Cedar denial counts in `unauthorized_calls`; a rate-limit or concurrency refusal counts in `throttled`. `MCP.stats()` returns those counters plus `expired_sessions` by name, the shape `MessageBus.stats()` uses; `MCP.counters()` layers that mapping over the canonical `CounterSource` protocol. Mounting on `Wreath` registers the server with `metrics.collect`, while a standalone `Router` deployment passes it explicitly through `counter_sources`. Each outcome also names itself on the per-call Flight Recorder marker (`_mcp/record.py`), which is emitted through `wreath.logging` -- the site is re-interned when the installed runtime's registry moves, because a site interned at import belongs to whichever registry was installed then. Argument *values* follow `wreath.logging`'s deny-by-default rule and argument *names* follow `crud.SENSITIVE_FIELD`; there is no MCP-specific redaction code and there must not be. `MCPAuth` (`_mcp/auth.py`) serves RFC 9728 metadata at `metadata_path_for(path)` -- the well-known segment is *inserted before* the endpoint path, not appended -- reuses `_auth/oauth2.bearer_challenge` (extended, never duplicated) for the RFC 6750 challenge, and performs the `aud` check itself rather than trusting the verifier's `audience=`, because a misconfigured verifier has no symptom until it is exploited. Sessions are bound to the subject that opened them and expire on idle (`MCPLimits.session_idle_seconds`), swept on touch rather than by a background task. **The binding is resolved through whichever of the two ways in identified the caller**, and read that way on every later message: it used to record only the identity `MCPAuth` had published, so an application authenticating with its own `app.configure_auth(...)` backend -- the supported second way, and the one `expose_routes` exists for -- opened every session with `principal=None` and bound nothing, which made a leaked `Mcp-Session-Id` a credential another verified caller could drive that session's calls, `DELETE` and notification stream with. `MCP._initialize` therefore falls back to `_identify` when `MCPAuth` published nobody, and `MCP._owns` resolves the same way when the session it is checking *is* bound; an endpoint with neither has nobody to bind to and its sessions stay open to whoever holds the id, which is stated in the guide rather than left to be discovered (`tests/test_red_team_mcp.py`). Payload size is deliberately *not* in `MCPLimits`: it is `RequestLimits.max_body_bytes`, and a second ceiling would be a second place to forget. The legacy two-endpoint HTTP+SSE transport is out of scope permanently. **`GET` now opens the session's notification stream** (it answered 405 through stage 2, deliberately, because there was nothing to send): one per session, a second is 409, the queue is bounded by `MCPLimits.max_pending_notifications` and a drop is counted in `notifications_dropped` rather than swallowed, the close sentinel evicts the oldest to guarantee delivery, and the generator emits an SSE comment every `stream_keepalive_seconds` because nothing in `SSEResponse` is on a timer. **Progress is `wreath.progress` relayed, never a second mechanism**: `ToolContext.progress` is an ordinary `ProgressReporter` on a `ProgressRegistry` the deployment may supply (a bus-backed one makes it fleet-wide), a watcher task polls `ProgressRegistry.stream` only when the call carried `_meta.progressToken`, and the entry is seeded at 0% first because `stream` gives up on a task id that never appears. A resource is gated on **its own URI** as the Cedar resource and a prompt on its own name, because both have a stable identity and a tool does not. Prompt arguments are refused at registration unless they are strings, since MCP carries them as a string map. **`Tool.policy` became `Tool.requirement: AuthRequirement`** so `expose_routes` can hand a route's merged requirement (`definition.requirement` + `requirement_for(endpoint)`) through unchanged -- authenticated, second factor, roles, permissions and policies are all enforced in `MCP._authorize`, and `_identify` falls back to the app's own auth backend so a route protected by a session backend still works. **That fallback runs before the rate limit is charged and before the audit marker is written**, not after: `_tools_call` (and `_sampling`/`_elicit` for a gate declared only on `sampling=`/`elicitation=`) calls `_identify` whenever the tool has a limiter or a non-zero `access_level`. It used to run only inside `_authorize`, so on an endpoint with no `MCPAuth` a per-tool ceiling keyed on the session was reset by a free `initialize` (1/hour admitted 6 calls) and the marker said `anonymous` for a caller the same request authorized as `User::ada`. The laziness is the point of the condition: an ungated, unbounded tool still never runs the backend; exposing a route must never be a hole around what was in front of it. `expose_routes` takes `tags=`/`include=`/`predicate=` and **has no `all=True`, permanently**; it refuses a route with no docstring and one whose signature a call cannot fill, naming the route as well as the parameter (`derive_input_schema` is passed the route path precisely so a placeholder is classified and refused rather than becoming an argument). **It also refuses a route carrying its own `middleware=` or `dependencies=`**, because a tool invokes the handler and does not replay the route's chain: those two are controls somebody put on that route -- a `before` hook returning a `403`, a `Depends(require_api_key)` that raises -- and carrying `definition.requirement` while dropping them silently published the handler to a model with strictly less in front of it than the HTTP path had. Refusing is the answer here, and it leaves running them later open where admitting the call would not; application middleware from `app.add_middleware(...)` is not in `definition.middleware` and already covers the endpoint, so nothing is refused for a control it still has (`tests/test_red_team_mcp.py`). **Error codes were renumbered once**: `-32002` is now the specification's own `RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND`, and Wreath's `RATE_LIMITED`/`TOO_MANY_CALLS` moved to `-32003`/`-32004` -- the collision was real, since the resources chapter names -32002 and clients special-case it. **Stage 4 shipped sampling, elicitation, roots, completions and the stdio wrapper, and every one of them reuses rather than adds.** The new machinery is `_mcp/outbound.py`: server-to-client *requests* need correlation, which stage 3's `GET` stream did not carry, so a `ClientChannel` per session holds a bounded pending table (`MCPLimits.max_pending_requests`) keyed on ids prefixed `wreath-` (JSON-RPC gives each direction its own id space). `Message` now carries `result`/`error` and `_post` routes a response into that table. **The reentrancy is the sharp edge and it works only because a `tools/call` already runs in its own task**: the answer arrives on a *different* POST while the call is parked, so a design that ran the call inline on the POST's coroutine would deadlock -- `tests/test_mcp_outbound.py` pins that a tool that elicits mid-call completes, a client that never answers times out and is told to stop (`notifications/cancelled` on the withdrawn id), `notifications/cancelled` on the outer call cancels the inner one, and `SessionStore.discard` fails every outstanding future (`ClientChannel.fail_all`, needed because a `resources/read` awaits on the POST's own coroutine and is in nobody's `in_flight`).
