Ships zero JavaScript, which is what lets its CSP be `default-src 'none'` with no script-src and no nonce; do not add inline script without revisiting that. `wreath.middleware.CsrfPolicy` cannot protect these routes (header-only token, HTML forms cannot carry a header), so `csrf=(request) -> bool` is required before any write operation is generated -- this is a recorded gap, not a design preference. Route paths are literal per model, so a text primary key whose value is exactly `new` is shadowed by the create route. Three invariants the tests exist to hold: a field the principal may not read never reaches the template context (assert at the data boundary, never on rendered output -- the rendered assertion passes whichever branch fired); every admin write is attributed and no anonymous fallback exists; the generated pages carry zero `wreath.audit` accessibility errors *and* warnings, checked in the suite rather than by hand, with only the deployment-level header rules (compression, cache-control, security-headers, hsts) excluded because they name middleware the application mounts for every route.

subsystems.name: platform
subsystems.capability: A cross-tenant operator console: every tenant's migration state, dead letters, stalled passes and quota burn on one page, with impersonation that cannot exceed the user
subsystems.policy: Composes and never re-implements; `scim_router` is the precedent -- an adapter with no store of its own, so what it shows is what the system has. Three defects the hand-written version of this console always has are what the design is against. It **reads across tenants unbound**: the obvious implementation queries with the application's own role and a schema interpolated from the URL, which is the cross-tenant read `wreath.tenancy` prevents, reintroduced by the tool built to supervise it -- so `inspect()` binds that tenant's own context and a second binding inside one scope is refused. Its **impersonation grants more than the user held**: this is a delegation, so the permitted set is an *intersection* with what the user holds, which makes composition-never-grants arithmetic rather than policy; scope and TTL have no defaults, it cannot nest (a chain nobody can compute), it reaches Cedar as `impersonated_by` so a policy can forbid a destructive action under it, and it audits inside the granting transaction. Its **destructive actions have no confirmation**: deprovisioning wants the tenant name typed back, following `privacy.erase`. The action vocabulary is `platform:`-prefixed and disjoint from crud's, and an organisation-scoped principal is refused whatever roles it holds, because org roles are namespaced `<org>:<role>` exactly so one tenant's admin is never another's. A source that raises costs its column, not the page (as `metrics.collect` already does) and is **named** in `unavailable`, because a missing dead-letter count must not read like a low one. Bulk reports per key with no atomic verdict (`apply_fleet`'s property), is bounded, and converges when re-run. No JavaScript, so the CSP needs no nonce; a write needs `csrf=`, since CsrfPolicy is header-only and a form cannot carry a header.

subsystems.name: sync
subsystems.capability: Subscribe to a query: a bounded, principal-derived shape whose answer is re-evaluated on every committed write, so a row leaving it is an ordinary tombstone rather than an unbounded revocation search
subsystems.policy: A shape MUST declare a `limit`, and an unbounded one is refused where it is *declared* rather than at the first request -- an unbounded shape works perfectly against a small table and stops working silently against a large one, long after the line that caused it was written. The bound is load-bearing twice: it is the per-subscription memory bound (the held key set lives in the subscription), and it is what makes revocation tractable, because an answer of at most `limit` rows can be diffed against the last one so a key that left is a tombstone in `delta.removed`. There is no separate revocation path -- the hard case and the easy case run the same diff, which is why there is no revocation code that could be correct in tests and wrong in production. Evaluation truncates to the declared bound even if the shape function later returns more, so the memory bound does not depend on the shape staying honest between calls. Authorization is evaluated ON THE CHANGE, never on the subscription: the shape is a closure over the principal, rebuilt on every evaluation, so a subscription cannot outlive the permission that opened it -- and it is NOT a second authorization path, because the shape is an ordinary `Select` and the route opening the stream is gated the way any route is. READ-ONLY in v1 by design: no client write path, no CRDT, no conflict resolution; writes go through the ordinary route where validation, Cedar and the ORM already live, because the moment two clients can write one field Wreath owns merge semantics forever. The doorbell is `wreath._livedoc` (bounded per-principal registry that refuses rather than evicts, cleanup on disconnect, cross-worker fan-out over `_orm_events`) and this module re-implements none of it; the signal is model-grained and means only *something moved, go and look* -- it is NEVER the delta, which is what keeps the answer correct under a write arriving out of order, twice, or from another worker, since the answer is always recomputed rather than patched. `watch=[...]` names other models whose writes move the answer; forgetting one is the bug where a revocation is noticed only the next time the row itself changes. A stream takes a session FACTORY, never a session: it may be open for hours and idle for most of them, so it must not hold a connection (a hundred tabs would exhaust a pool of twenty) and must not hold a session (one opened before the write would re-read its own identity map and report nothing changed). Row versions use keyed blake2b rather than `hash()`, which is randomised per process -- two workers would otherwise disagree about whether a row moved and a client hopping between them would see spurious upserts forever. A failed evaluation does not end the stream and is counted in `stale_evaluations()`; a shape broken since deploy is otherwise indistinguishable from one whose answer never changes. NOT BUILT: resumption from a durable cursor. A reconnecting client is sent a fresh `snapshot` whose key set is authoritative (the tombstone rule applied wholesale, one bounded query). Resuming instead needs a row-grained change feed appended INSIDE the writing transaction, which is `wreath.audit_log`'s ORM-session hook rather than one this module may add; `docs/reference/roadmap.md` carries the row.

subsystems.name: xml
subsystems.capability: A strict XML profile and Exclusive XML Canonicalization 1.0 for documents that carry a signature -- the prerequisite for SAML, owned here because defusedxml and xmlsec are third-party runtime dependencies and the stdlib has C14N 2.0 rather than the exclusive algorithm XML Signature requires, and the SAML 2.0 assertion verification built on it
subsystems.policy: The refusals are the feature, and widening the profile is a security change rather than a convenience one. No DTD in any form -- that is the only entity declaration site, so refusing it removes XXE, billion laughs and quadratic blowup as a class instead of as three checks. No comments and no CDATA: both give one value two readings, which is how a signed <NameID> gets truncated into a different identity. UTF-8 only, no BOM, no overlong or surrogate sequences -- one byte sequence, one meaning. Every element records the byte range it was parsed from, and canonicalization RE-READS THOSE BYTES rather than re-serializing the tree; that, plus find_id refusing a repeated identifier instead of resolving it by document order, is what makes XML Signature Wrapping unexpressible rather than merely checked for. Do not add an API that resolves an element a second way. There is one parser, and that is deliberate: two parsers that disagree is the same wrapping bug one layer down. It is held to the corpus on the tree, the spans, the canonical bytes and the reason AND message of every refusal (tests/test_xml_parse.py, test_xml_refusals.py, test_xml_c14n.py, test_xml_wrapping.py, test_xml_fuzz.py). max_depth is capped at MAX_DEPTH_CEILING because the C parser is recursive descent and an unbounded depth would be a caller-selectable stack overflow; keep MAX_DEPTH_CEILING in src/wreath/_xml_model.py -- where the tree, the bounds and XMLRefusal are defined once for both arms -- and XML_MAX_DEPTH_CEILING in _native/xml.c in step. This module verifies no signatures and knows nothing about SAML. `wreath.saml` is the service-provider *receiving* half only and decides nothing: a VerifiedAssertion's facts() is a Cedar context mapping, so 'verified' means the identity provider said this rather than that it is trusted -- the same split wreath.signatures makes. It sits on wreath.xml because that is what removes the XML-DSig dependency: verification canonicalizes by re-reading the source bytes an element was parsed from, so signature wrapping is unexpressible rather than checked for, and the transform list is an allow-list of exactly two because a transform the verifier ignores is one that changed what the digest covers. **It ships with no test module of its own** -- tests/_saml_fixtures.py is fixtures, not tests -- which is tracked as a gap rather than an omission.

subsystems.name: entity
subsystems.capability: Leased, fenced ownership of a name, and a question that reaches whoever holds one -- the addressing a stateful gateway needs behind a stateless load balancer
subsystems.policy: One name, one owner, one mailbox. `hold` is a single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE, so a returned row *is* the claim -- there is no read-then-write window in which two workers both conclude they were first, which is the argument wreath.store already makes for keyed state applied to names. The fence moves on a handover and never on a renewal, following wreath.jobs: a fence that moved on renewal would invalidate the holder's own in-flight work. `release` is scoped to the owner in the WHERE, so a lapsed holder tidying up on shutdown cannot delete its successor's row. This deliberately does NOT replace SingletonRunner: an advisory lock releases the instant its connection drops, which is a better failure detector than a lease and costs a held connection per name -- right for one-name, wrong for a hundred thousand. Two mechanisms for two shapes. `ask` decides NotHeld from the ownership table *before* publishing, because an ephemeral publish to nobody is a silent no-op and waiting a full deadline to learn that is a bad diagnosis; NotHeld and Unanswered stay separate exceptions because a missing device and a wedged worker want different operator responses. The transport is ephemeral fan-out, so a timeout is an ordinary outcome rather than an error. One channel per registry, never one per name -- a channel per entity is a LISTEN per entity and the case this exists for is a hundred thousand of them -- so every worker sees every message and the filtering is load-bearing rather than decorative. A holder re-checks ownership before answering, because the name can move between the asker's check and the message arriving. The pending map is bounded and refusals counted: it is memory a remote caller would otherwise control. The renewal tick is **one statement however many names a worker holds** (`WHERE owner = $1`), because a statement per name per tick is a round trip per entity per tick, which is the cost that stops this scaling; the RETURNING set is also the only way to learn a name was taken, since there is no heartbeat. A lost name is dropped locally so a later release cannot delete the new holder's row, and counted -- non-zero `lost` is what distinguishes shedding ownership from clients reconnecting. `grace=` defers a release onto the same tick rather than a timer per name, so a reconnect renews instead of handing the name over and taking it back. Drain releases everything in one statement: a lease is sized for crash detection, where waiting is the only option, and a clean shutdown has better information than that. `release_many` builds `IN ($2, $3, ...)` per call rather than binding an array to `= ANY($1)`: the driver refuses to bind a sequence on purpose, since `[1, 2]` is equally int4[]/int8[]/numeric[] and `[]` names no element type. That costs a plan and saves a round trip per name, on a path that runs only when a grace period expires. The bug was invisible to the unit suite -- a fake never binds -- and surfaced on first contact with a real server.
